summaries.Q160659: Ferris wheel installed for the celebrations of the year 2000, at the same time as the Millennium Dome in Greenwich. Built flat over the Thames, it was raised upright at the cost of several days of effort, a first attempt having failed. Its 32 capsules complete a turn in about 24 min 30 s.
summaries.Q41225: Strictly speaking the name is that of the largest bell of the chime; usage extends it to the clock and to the tower of the Palace of Westminster, called the Clock Tower and then the Elizabeth Tower since Elizabeth II's diamond jubilee in 2012. About 96 metres high, it comes from Charles Barry's plan, chosen after the fire at Parliament in 1834.
summaries.Q106509908: Painted by volunteers from March 2021, this mural runs for more than five hundred metres along the south bank of the Thames, facing the Palace of Westminster and in front of St Thomas' Hospital. It lines up thousands of red and pink hearts, meant to count one for each Covid victim recorded in the United Kingdom at its launch.
summaries.Q1990172: An imagined reconstruction of 221B Baker Street, the fictional home of Arthur Conan Doyle's detective, this house museum opened on 27 March 1990 at 239 Baker Street, not far from the address in the novels. The decor, inspired by the 1984 television series, mixes wax figures and familiar objects. Royal Mail forwards mail addressed to 221B there.
summaries.Q739364: Seat of the Catholic archdiocese of Westminster, it is the largest Catholic place of worship in England and Wales. The land, previously occupied by a prison, was bought in 1884; building began in 1895 to plans by John Francis Bentley. Opened in 1903, it was not consecrated until 28 June 1910.
summaries.Q1346906: A large public garden in Bloomsbury, it owes its name to the earls and dukes of Bedford, whose family name is Russell. The British Museum and the main building of the University of London are close by, as is Russell Square Underground station. In 2002 the park was reworked to recover its original 19th century look.
summaries.Q1112579: This former City church was rebuilt after the Great Fire of 1666 following Christopher Wren's instructions. The area, linked to printing and then to the daily papers, made it the journalists' church. Bombed on 29 December 1940, it lost its nave, was raised again from 1953 and reopened on 19 December 1957.
summaries.Q55018: The third theatre built on this site, after a first one opened on 7 December 1732, it houses the Royal Opera, the Royal Ballet and the Orchestra of the Royal Opera House, and is now called Royal Ballet and Opera. The facade, the foyer and the auditorium date from 1858, almost all the rest from the 1990s. It can hold 2,268 people.
summaries.Q846686: A historic route linking the City of Westminster to the City of London, continuing the Strand, the street takes its name from the Fleet, a tributary of the Thames now covered over. Printers settled there from 1500 and the first British daily paper appeared there in 1702. The exodus of the press began in 1986 and ended in 2005.
summaries.Q83125: A bascule bridge built from 1886 to cross the Thames without closing the port to tall ships, it was opened on 30 June 1894 by the Prince of Wales. On the death of the architect Horace Jones, in 1887, George D. Stevenson took over the project and replaced the brick facade with neo-Gothic work matching the Tower of London.
summaries.Q171458: This ground in Walham Green, in the borough of Hammersmith and Fulham, is Chelsea's. Its name refers not to the battle of 1066 but to the bridge beside the main entrance. Opened on 28 April 1877, it stayed devoted to athletics until 1904, when Gus Mears bought it; Fulham having refused to come, he founded Chelsea.
summaries.Q216185: A crossing of six important streets, among them The Mall, Whitehall and The Strand, the place is taken as the heart of London: distances from London are counted from the equestrian statue of Charles I, and the junction serves as the zero point for the United Kingdom. Trafalgar Square borders its north side.
summaries.Q7275188: Raised in Green Park, this memorial commemorates the 55,573 airmen of RAF Bomber Command during the Second World War, whatever their nationality. It was unveiled by Queen Elizabeth II on 28 June 2012.
summaries.Q622206: Built from 1771 to 1778 by Robert Adam for Baron Apsley, this Piccadilly house, facing Hyde Park Corner, was bought in 1807 by Richard Wellesley, who passed it in 1817 to his brother Arthur, 1st Duke of Wellington, who commissioned the Corinthian portico. Given to the state in 1947, it holds the Wellington Museum and 200 paintings.
summaries.Q565521: Built from 1825 to 1827 to plans by John Nash for William, Duke of Clarence, this royal house on the Mall adjoins St James's Palace, with which it shares a garden. Home of the Queen Mother from 1953 to 2002, it is today that of Charles III and Queen Camilla, and opens to visitors for about two months each summer.
summaries.Q1574424: Opened in 1832 on the model of Père Lachaise, this Anglican cemetery of 29 hectares is one of London's seven great historic cemeteries, the Magnificent Seven. It has more than 65,000 graves, mausoleums, vaults and catacombs, holding about 250,000 bodies, among them those of Charles Babbage and Thackeray.
summaries.Q1093271: Founded in 1123 as an Augustinian priory by Rahere, this Anglican church in Smithfield keeps the most significant Romanesque interior architecture in the City of London. More than half of the priory church was destroyed in 1543; spared by the great fire of 1666, it was restored by Aston Webb at the end of the 19th century.
summaries.Q193639: Work on this South Kensington hall began on 20 May 1867; it was opened on 29 March 1871 and owes its name to Prince Albert, at the request of his widow Queen Victoria. A terracotta frieze of 244 m, The Triumph of Arts and Sciences, runs along the facade. The BBC Proms have been held there every summer since 1941.
summaries.Q804402: Laid out in the 18th century at the initiative of William Baker, whose name it bears, this City of Westminster street was first lived in by high society. Conan Doyle placed Sherlock Holmes and Doctor Watson there at 221B, a number that does not exist. The Special Operations Executive had its headquarters there during the Second World War.
summaries.Q130206: A wooden bridge already crossed the Thames under Roman occupation, in the time of Londinium. A stone structure of 19 arches, built from 1176 to 1209, followed it, carrying houses until 1770. John Rennie's granite bridge of 1831 was dismantled in 1969 and re-erected at Lake Havasu City, Arizona. The present bridge dates from 1973.
summaries.Q18536: An office and luxury housing skyscraper in Southwark, on the south bank of the Thames, with Renzo Piano as architect. At its opening, on 5 July 2012, its 309.60 m made it the tallest building in the United Kingdom and in the European Union. It opened to the public on 1 February 2013, two floors being kept for paying visits.
summaries.Q842089: Overlooking Trafalgar Square, the statue of Admiral Horatio Nelson crowns a Corinthian column of granite and bronze, 44 metres high, built between 1840 and 1843. William Railton designed the upper part and the statue, which Edward Hodges Baily sculpted. Four bronze lions, by Edwin Landseer in 1867, adorn the base.
summaries.Q6373: Founded in 1753, notably from the collection bequeathed by the physician Hans Sloane, it opened to the public on 15 January 1759 at Montagu House, in Bloomsbury, on the same site as today. Its collections, of more than seven million objects from every continent, are among the largest in the world.
summaries.Q2002512: Attached to University College London, on Malet Place, this Egyptology museum keeps more than 80,000 objects. Its core comes from the collection given in 1892 by Amelia Edwards; the first professor of Egyptology, William Matthew Flinders Petrie, sold the produce of his excavations to UCL in 1913. Entry is free.
summaries.Q1093950: Seat of the Greater London Authority until its move to Newham in 2022, the building stands on the south bank of the Thames, near Tower Bridge. Designed by Norman Foster, it was opened in July 2002. 45 metres high with ten floors, bulb shaped, it was nicknamed the glass testicle by the former mayor Ken Livingstone.
summaries.Q926913: Created by an Act of Parliament in 1839 under the name West of London and Westminster Cemetery, it was consecrated in June 1840 and is one of the Magnificent Seven, seven cemeteries opened around London in the 19th century. Designed by the architect Benjamin Baud, it lines up some 35,000 monuments for 205,000 people buried.
summaries.Q579381: Founded in 675 by the abbot of the monastery of Barking, this Anglican church in the City of London keeps a 2nd century Roman floor in its crypt. Its tower, destroyed in 1650 by the explosion of powder barrels, was rebuilt in 1658. The church escaped the great fire of 1666, Admiral William Penn having had the neighbouring houses pulled down.
summaries.Q272434: Raised in 1599 in Southwark, the first Globe housed Shakespeare's company, the Lord Chamberlain's Men. It burned on 29 June 1613 during a performance of Henry VIII, was rebuilt on the same spot and reopened the next year, before being closed by the Puritans in 1642, then demolished in 1644. The present theatre, built in 1996, opened in 1997.
summaries.Q756819: This street runs from Charing Cross north east to the boundary of the City, marked by Temple Bar, where Fleet Street takes over. Its name comes from the Old English for shore: before the Embankment was built, it ran along the Thames. It originally linked the City to the centre of royal power at Westminster, then two separate cities.
summaries.Q456960: Opened in 1862, this seven arch iron bridge replaced a first structure of 1750. Some of its Gothic ornaments are by Charles Barry, the architect of the Palace of Westminster. The dominant green is that of the leather seats in the House of Commons, while Lambeth Bridge, upstream, is red like the seats of the House of Lords.
summaries.Q191161: This City skyscraper stands on the former site of the Baltic Exchange. Opened on 28 April 2004, designed by Norman Foster's practice for Swiss Re, it has 41 floors for 180 metres, and its aerodynamic shape helps ventilate the building. Londoners call it the Gherkin, after that shape.
summaries.Q60308: A Roman wall raised around Londinium, the largest town of the Roman province of Britain. A few sections of it survive. About 3.2 kilometres long and some 6 metres high, it enclosed 130 hectares now largely within the City of London. Its gates have left their names to places in London: Ludgate, Newgate, Aldgate.
summaries.Q42182: Official residence of the British sovereigns, in the City of Westminster. Its core is a town house built for the Duke of Buckingham John Sheffield, bought by George III in 1762, then enlarged mainly by John Nash and Edward Blore. The palace became the residence of the monarchy at Victoria's accession to the throne, in 1837.
summaries.Q591086: Two contemporary art museums in Kensington Gardens, separated by the Serpentine lake that gives them their name. The Serpentine Gallery, founded in 1970, occupies a former tea pavilion of 1933-1934; the Serpentine Sackler Gallery, opened in 2013, reuses a gunpowder store of 1805 with an extension by Zaha Hadid.
summaries.Q565532: Seat of the Commonwealth of Nations and of its Secretariat, this St James's mansion was built for Sarah Churchill, Duchess of Marlborough: Christopher Wren and his son drew up the plans, before the duchess dismissed them and took over the design. The Crown has leased it to the Commonwealth Secretariat since 1965.
summaries.Q932992: Laid out in 1720 by members of the Grosvenor family, whose name it bears, and built between 1725 and 1731, this Mayfair square is, apart from Lincoln's Inn Fields, the largest public square in London. Its garden, reserved for residents, only opened to the public in 1946. The United States embassy sat there from 1938 to 2017.
summaries.Q385521: Built from 1630 to 1633 by Inigo Jones at the request of Francis Russell, 4th Earl of Bedford, it is the first church built in London since the Reformation. A simple chapel of the parish of St Martin-in-the-Fields, it was dedicated to St Paul in 1645, when Covent Garden became a parish in its own right. It is also called the Actor's Church.
summaries.Q511108: On the south bank, in Lambeth, the brutalist building designed by Denys Lasdun opened its three auditoriums between 1976 and 1977; until then the company played at the Old Vic. In opinion polls it is at once the most liked and the most disliked building in London.
summaries.Q1123106: A West End shopping street by the architect John Nash, it links Waterloo Place to Mortimer Street by way of Piccadilly Circus and Oxford Circus. It took its name, that of the Prince Regent and future George IV, in January 1819 and opened without ceremony at the end of the summer of the same year. Hamleys and Liberty have shops there.
summaries.Q44057: This steel footbridge crosses the Thames between Southwark and the City; its supports frame the view of the south front of St Paul's Cathedral. Opened on 10 June 2000, it closed three days later, the crowd making it sway sideways, hence its nickname the Wobbly Bridge. Dampers settled the problem; it reopened in February 2002.
summaries.Q927198: The Roman town at the origin of London, founded after the invasion of 43 led by the emperor Claudius, but which archaeologists date rather to around 50. The site was chosen where the banks of the Thames are closest, in order to build a bridge there, the river staying deep enough for ships. The town covered about 1.4 km2.
summaries.Q359256: A monumental arch built in 1911 to plans by Aston Webb, at the instigation of Edward VII and in memory of his mother Queen Victoria; the king died before the work was finished. The central archway, closed by a wrought iron gate, is used only by the sovereign at official ceremonies.
summaries.Q62378: A fortress on the north bank of the Thames, whose building began at the end of 1066, as part of the Norman conquest. The White Tower, raised on the order of William the Conqueror in 1078, gave the whole its name. The castle served as a prison from 1100, but also as a royal palace and armoury; it holds the Crown Jewels.
summaries.Q1311497: A contemporary art museum created by Charles Saatchi in 1985, first set up in Boundary Road, in north London, then at County Hall in April 2003, and finally in Chelsea. After showing American and minimalist artists, the gallery sold that collection to back, from 1990, the Young British Artists, among them Damien Hirst.
summaries.Q69482: This Inn of Court, next to the Royal Courts of Justice, remains one of the four training centres for barristers. Its founding date is unknown, its records go back to 1422. In 1234 a decree of Henry III banned law schools in the City; the lawyers moved to Holborn, where the Earl of Lincoln had invited them onto his land.
summaries.Q1936696: A Bloomsbury square that owes its name to Francis Russell, Marquess of Tavistock; only the houses on the west side, by Thomas Cubitt, have survived. The park brings together a statue of Mahatma Gandhi installed in 1968, a memorial to conscientious objectors and a bust of Virginia Woolf. On 7 July 2005 a suicide bombing there killed 14.
summaries.Q1570699: An independent Baptist church, founded in Southwark in 1650 under the name New Park Street Chapel. Charles Spurgeon became its pastor in 1854; the congregation moved in 1861 to Elephant and Castle, into a building with an auditorium of 6,000 seats. Burnt several times, the building was rebuilt in 1894, 1941 and 1959, with 1,750 seats.
summaries.Q868806: Founded in 1818, this theatre near Waterloo station was taken over in 1880 by Emma Cons, then in 1898 by her niece Lilian Baylis, who began in 1914 to produce Shakespeare plays there. In 1963 it formed the core of the Royal National Theatre company, which stayed until new premises were built on the south bank, in 1976.
summaries.Q925349: A City of Westminster street parallel to The Mall, known for the gentlemen's clubs founded in the 19th and 20th centuries, among them the Athenaeum and the Reform Club, and nicknamed Club Land. The name comes from paille-maille, a French mallet game played nearby in the 17th century. It was the world's first gas lit street, on 28 January 1807.
summaries.Q501003: A road bridge over the Thames, near Waterloo station. The first structure on the site, by John Rennie, opened in 1817 as a toll bridge; the French ambassador refused to attend the opening, the name recalling the battle of Waterloo. In the 1920s the London County Council decided to replace it with a bridge by Giles Gilbert Scott.
summaries.Q331613: A cricket ground in St John's Wood, owned by the Marylebone Cricket Club, it bears the name of its founder Thomas Lord, who set it up after the line of the Regent's Canal cut across the playing area of his previous ground. The opening match took place there on 22 June 1814. England have played test matches there since 1884.
summaries.Q281465: Raised in Kensington Gardens, facing the Royal Albert Hall, in memory of Albert of Saxe-Coburg and Gotha, husband of Queen Victoria, this neo-Gothic monument by George Gilbert Scott is 47.5 metres high. The structure was finished in 1872 and the gilded statue set in place in 1875: Albert holds a catalogue of the Great Exhibition of 1851.
summaries.Q23308: National library of the United Kingdom, founded in 1973: before that, the role belonged to the British Museum. Its Euston Road building, opened in 1997 and by the architect Colin St John Wilson, is the largest public building put up in the United Kingdom in the 20th century. A glass tower holds the King's Library, gathered by George III.
summaries.Q2060860: Housed in the former home of the neoclassical architect John Soane (1753-1837), this eclectic museum brings together drawings, prints, paintings, furniture and antiquities. It shows canvases by William Hogarth, among them the series A Rake's Progress, as well as works by Canaletto, Watteau and Turner.
summaries.Q2914560: Headquarters of the BBC, in Portland Place, it is the very first broadcasting centre in the United Kingdom specially designed as such. It was opened on 15 May 1932.
summaries.Q2893581: Built between 1775 and 1783, this Bloomsbury square owes its name to the title of the Russell family, dukes of Bedford and large landowners in the area. Its design is generally attributed to Thomas Leverton. The doorways of the brick houses are dressed with Coade stone and the central garden remains private.
summaries.Q4893186: Designed by Christopher Wren, appointed architect in 1672, this Anglican church in Piccadilly was consecrated on 13 July 1684 by Henry Compton, Bishop of London. In red brick, it keeps a marble font and a limewood reredos by Grinling Gibbons. Badly damaged by the Blitz in 1940, it was restored up to 1954.
summaries.Q1155331: Its name changes with the sex of the monarch: Her Majesty's Theatre in 1837, His Majesty's in 1901, Her Majesty's in 1952, then His Majesty's after the coronation of Charles III. A theatre has stood on the site since 1705; the present building, the fourth, opened in 1897. It has given The Phantom of the Opera since 1986.
summaries.Q1368556: A square at the north west end of the Palace of Westminster, framed by Westminster Abbey, St Margaret's church and the Middlesex Guildhall, seat of the Supreme Court. Eleven statues of politicians stand there, among them those of Churchill and Mandela. Since May 2018 that of the suffragist Millicent Fawcett has been added.
summaries.Q1324578: Crossing the Thames between Southwark, on the south bank, and the City, it is one of the four bridges run by the Lord Mayor's services. A first structure was built there from 1814 to 1819, replaced by a five span steel bridge raised from 1912 to 1921. It stands between the Millennium Bridge and the Cannon Street Railway Bridge.
summaries.Q209651: Created by EMI in November 1931 in a former town house in Abbey Road, these recording studios were at first meant for classical music. The Beatles recorded most of their songs there from 1962 to 1969, and in 1976 the studios took the name of the group's last album. Pink Floyd, Oasis and Radiohead have worked there.
summaries.Q607700: This Doric column of Portland stone, 61 metres high, commemorates the great fire of 1666: its height matches the distance separating it from the bakery in Pudding Lane where the fire began. Designed by Christopher Wren and Robert Hooke, it holds a central shaft first meant for astronomy and a stair of 311 steps.
summaries.Q180788: Founded in 1824, the gallery grew out of the purchase of the thirty-eight paintings of John Julius Angerstein and has occupied the north side of Trafalgar Square since 1838. Its permanent collection of 2,300 paintings, dating from 1250 to 1900, belongs to the British state and is free to visit; only temporary exhibitions are paid for.
summaries.Q1786933: Official residence of the Lord Mayor of the City of London, it was built from 1739 to 1752 by George Dance the Elder, on the site of the church of St Mary Woolchurch Haw destroyed in the great fire. The Lord Mayor tries offences committed in the City there, hence eleven cells. It keeps 84 Dutch and Flemish paintings of the 17th century.
summaries.Q157412: This society of barristers and judges is one of the four Inns of Court of London: one must belong to one of them to practise as a barrister in England and Wales. Lawyers have been established there since at least 1370, but none of the four claims to be older than the others. The gardens have existed since 1597 at least.
summaries.Q782140: From the 17th century to the middle of the 19th, this Islington burial ground was used for the burial of nonconformists. It holds the graves of William Blake, of Daniel Defoe, of John Bunyan, author of The Pilgrim's Progress, of George Fox, one of the founders of the Quaker movement, and of the statistician Thomas Bayes.
summaries.Q536866: The second church of this name, it was the first of the fifty new churches commissioned in London in 1711. Its building began in 1714 under the direction of James Gibbs, and it was consecrated on 1 January 1723. Gibbs planned a column carrying a statue of Queen Anne; on her death the stone was used to build a steeple.
summaries.Q1756626: The present building dates from 1812 and closes a series of four houses raised on the same spot since 1663, which makes it the oldest theatre in London. The front faces Catherine Street, the back Drury Lane. A patent theatre, it shared a royal monopoly on spoken plays. Today it mostly stages musicals.
summaries.Q510323: This area in the north east of Hyde Park is set aside for public speaking: anyone may take a temporary speaker's role before whoever is there at the time. It was not until 1872 that the government recognised this need to meet in public to debate. London has others, at Finsbury Park, Clapham Common and Victoria Park.
summaries.Q1130666: This road and foot bridge of five steel arches was opened on 12 July 1932 by George V and Queen Mary. The red of its paint is that of the benches of the House of Lords, close to the bridge. The obelisks at its ends carry pineapples, in tribute to John Tradescant, said to have brought the first pineapple to Great Britain.
summaries.Q1155836: A cricket ground in Kennington, sometimes called Kennington Oval, it owes its name to its oval shape and has changed official name several times with its partners. It hosts the Surrey team and the last test match of the season on English soil; 20 FA Cup finals have been held there.
summaries.Q1333411: Raised in honour of Queen Victoria, this monument faces the gates of the main entrance of Buckingham Palace, at the west end of the Mall. The sculptor Thomas Brock made it in 1911 with the help of the architect Aston Webb; 25 m high, it took 2,300 tonnes of white marble. A winged Victory in gilded bronze crowns it.
summaries.Q186309: Founded in 1835 by the French artist Marie Tussaud, trained in sculpture by Philippe Curtius, this wax museum first opened in Baker Street; the Chamber of Horrors is one of its main attractions. It moved in 1884 to Marylebone Road, its present site, where a fire destroyed many figures in 1925.
summaries.Q1541098: Housed in Covent Garden in an iron and glass hall designed in 1871 as a flower market by William Rogers, it has occupied the place since 1980, the market having moved in 1971. It keeps and explains the capital's transport heritage. Its Acton depot, opened in 1999, holds more than 370,000 objects.
summaries.Q1194829: The central criminal court of the British Crown, between Holborn Circus and St Paul's Cathedral, it tries the main criminal cases of Greater London. The present building, designed by Edward William Mountford on the site of Newgate prison, was opened by Edward VII in 1907. A statue of Justice crowns its dome.
summaries.Q5933: A Gothic church in London, dating for the most part from the 13th century, when Henry III rebuilt it to give a setting to the tomb of Edward the Confessor. Since William the Conqueror, in 1066, the sovereigns have been crowned there, with two exceptions. More than 3,300 people are buried there; UNESCO listed since 1987.
summaries.Q11704046: An Anglican church of the City of London, next to the Guildhall, built in the 12th century near the old medieval ghetto centred on Old Jewry. Destroyed by the great fire of 1666, it was rebuilt by Christopher Wren between 1670 and 1677. Its gridiron shaped weathervane refers to the martyrdom of St Lawrence.
summaries.Q676755: A Westminster theatre, in Argyll Street, put up in 1910 by Walter Gibbons on a site that had carried a bazaar, then a circus, then an ice rink, it has 2,286 seats and has been Grade II* listed since 1960. This variety house has hosted the Royal Variety Performance 43 times and, from 1955 to 1967, a Sunday ITV show.
summaries.Q892187: A Mayfair shopping street, in the City of Westminster, it links Piccadilly to Oxford Street and owes its name to the baronet Thomas Bond, behind the development of the area. It in fact joins two ways: Old Bond Street, laid out around 1686, and New Bond Street, opened in 1700-1720. Its luxury shops are known worldwide.
summaries.Q880843: A City bridge crossing the Thames near the Inns of Court and Tate Modern, it is one of the four bridges run by the Lord Mayor's services. The first structure, in Portland stone arches, opened in 1769; the present iron bridge of 281 m, designed by Joseph Cubitt, replaced it in 1869. The banker Roberto Calvi was found hanged there in 1982.
summaries.Q1344889: This large neoclassical building faces the Strand, on the left bank of the Thames, just north of Waterloo Bridge. It replaces Old Somerset House, a palatial group begun in the 1550s and demolished from 1775. The present central part, by William Chambers, was built between 1776 and 1796.
summaries.Q526804: Commissioned by George IV in 1825 to commemorate the British victories of the Napoleonic wars, this triumphal arch was built from 1826 to 1830 to plans by Decimus Burton. Moved between 1882 and 1883 to allow the streets to be widened, it occupies the centre of the Hyde Park Corner roundabout. A bronze quadriga has crowned it since 1912.
summaries.Q213322: Set in South Kensington, this national art museum is devoted to applied and decorative arts, to design and to sculpture. Founded in 1852, it bears the name of Queen Victoria and of her husband Prince Albert. It covers five hectares and has 145 galleries, for a permanent collection of more than 2.27 million objects.
summaries.Q571249: Founded in 1989 by Terence Conran in a converted warehouse in Bermondsey, on the south bank of the Thames, this museum is devoted to contemporary architecture and design. It moved in 2016 to Kensington, south of Holland Park, into the former Commonwealth Institute, a building of the 1960s.
summaries.Q81279: Built between 1411 and 1440, this building was for centuries the town hall of the City of London, of which it remains the administrative centre. It is the only non religious medieval building to have survived in the City. Frederic Chopin played there before the public for the last time on 16 November 1848.
summaries.Q173882: Raised after the destruction of the previous building in the great fire of 1666, it crowns Ludgate Hill, site of four earlier churches. It is taken as Christopher Wren's masterpiece; the first stone was laid in 1675. Its dome, made of three shells one inside another, tops out at 111.3 metres, after 528 steps.
summaries.Q2323930: This Anglican church of the Barbican Estate, in the City of London, is dedicated to Giles the Hermit. When it was built it stood outside (without) the London wall, near Cripplegate. Rebuilt in perpendicular Gothic in 1394, it survived the great fire of 1666. John Milton was buried there in 1674.
summaries.Q647390: This Southbank Centre concert hall, built after the Second World War to plans by Robert Matthew and Leslie Martin, was opened on 3 May 1951 as part of the Festival of Britain. Fully refurbished in 2005, it has the London Philharmonic Orchestra and the Philharmonia Orchestra in residence.
summaries.Q1254964: This large parade ground extends behind Whitehall, in the City of Westminster. Under Henry VIII the jousts of Whitehall Palace were held there. Since the 17th century it has hosted military reviews and parades, among them Trooping the Colour, which marks the birthday of the reigning sovereign, and Beating Retreat.
summaries.Q1142134: Second bridge on the site, it links Westminster and Pimlico, on the north bank, to Vauxhall on the south. Its predecessor, the first cast iron bridge over the Thames, opened in May 1813 and was demolished in 1898. Opened on 26 May 1906 by the Prince of Wales, it carries eight statues of women by Frederick Pomeroy and Alfred Drury on its abutments.
summaries.Q1331574: Built for the National Westminster Bank, this skyscraper at 25 Old Broad Street was originally called the NatWest Tower: seen from above, it repeats the shape of the bank's logo, three chevrons in a hexagonal arrangement. Designed by Richard Seifert, it was raised between 1971 and 1979 and opened in 1980. The Vertigo 42 bar occupies its top.
summaries.Q1858077: A square tower of 98.5 metres and 14 floors, it occupies the south west end of the Palace of Westminster and bears the name of Queen Victoria. It holds the Parliamentary Archives of both houses, called before 2006 the House of Lords Record Office. Its mast carries the national flag, replaced by the royal standard when the king is in the palace.
summaries.Q193375: Opened on 13 May 2000 in a disused power station at Bankside, in Southwark, the museum brings together the national collection of modern and contemporary art from the Tate Gallery. The conversion was given in 1995 to Herzog & de Meuron, who turned the turbine hall into a huge space and designed the extension opened in June 2016.
summaries.Q1024854: One of the five branches of the Imperial War Museum, between Whitehall and Horse Guards Road, the museum brings together the Cabinet War Rooms, an underground complex that housed a command centre during the Second World War, and a museum devoted to Winston Churchill. Decommissioned in 1945, it was little used until the museum opened in 1984.
summaries.Q1451262: The Catholic cathedral of the archdiocese of Southwark, distinct from the Anglican Southwark Cathedral, it faces the Imperial War Museum. Designed by Augustus Pugin, it opened in 1848 and was the first Catholic cathedral built in the United Kingdom since the Reformation. Bombed during the war, it reopened rebuilt in 1958.
summaries.Q823412: Parish church of the Palace of Westminster since 1614, it stands within the abbey precinct. Founded in the 12th century by the Benedictines, rebuilt from 1486 to 1523, it was reworked inside by George Gilbert Scott in 1877. A Flemish window of 1509 commemorates the betrothal of Catherine of Aragon to Henry VIII.
summaries.Q332474: A luxury department store in Brompton Road, Knightsbridge, it is the largest in London and its motto is Omnia Ubique omnibus, everything, everywhere, for everyone. Born in 1849 of the grocery of Charles Henry Harrod, it came under the control of the Al-Fayed family in 1985 through the purchase of House of Fraser, then sold in 2010 to Qatar Holding.
summaries.Q1337772: A Hammersmith concert hall opened in 1932 under the name Gaumont Palace, it owes its Art Deco decoration to Cromie and has changed name several times, Hammersmith Odeon in 1962, Eventim Apollo in 2013. Its reputation was made in the 1960s and many concerts were recorded there, among them Iron Maiden's Beast over Hammersmith.
summaries.Q620182: A tree lined crescent street, about 500 m long, it meets the Strand at both its ends and takes in Kingsway at its middle. Laid out with that avenue at the beginning of the 20th century, it stands on the site of Lundenwic, a 7th century Anglo-Saxon settlement. Bush House, home of the BBC World Service from 1941 to 2012, lines it.
summaries.Q1972207: A road bridge between Chelsea and Battersea, opened in 1873 to plans by Rowland Mason Ordish, it proved barely solid: Bazalgette strengthened it from 1884 to 1887, then the Greater London Council added two piers in 1973. Its toll booths are the only ones left on a London bridge and its shaking earned it the nickname Trembling Lady.
summaries.Q797085: A British Telecom telecommunications tower, in Fitzrovia, it was opened by Prime Minister Harold Wilson on 8 October 1965 and opened to the public on 16 May 1966. A bomb of the Angry Brigade group went off in its toilets on 31 October 1971; public access was banned in 1981 for security reasons.
summaries.Q180887: A monumental spider by Louise Bourgeois, dedicated to her mother, about 10 metres high, carrying under its body a sac of twenty-six marble eggs. Commissioned for the artist's opening contribution to the Unilever Series, this is the original version, in stainless steel: first on long loan, it was acquired by Tate in January 2008.
summaries.Q309388: Set along Exhibition Road, in Kensington, it keeps about 70 million specimens of life and earth sciences, among them the collections brought by James Cook and Charles Darwin. The terracotta brick building, with neo-Romanesque fronts by Alfred Waterhouse, was built from 1873 to 1880; the museum opened in 1881.
summaries.Q1513107: An attraction run by the Merlin Entertainments group, housed at County Hall near the London Eye, it stages bloody historical events with actors and special effects: the great plague, Jack the Ripper, the torture chamber. Opened in 1976 in Tooley Street, it reopened on 1 March 2013.
summaries.Q225471: In 1664 Richard Boyle, first Earl of Burlington, wanted a town house built for himself near St James's. The third earl had the whole rebuilt in the Palladian style with Colen Campbell, then the house was altered from 1867 to 1873 in the neo-Renaissance style. The Piccadilly building has housed the Royal Academy since 1868.
summaries.Q1335201: An Anglican church at the north east corner of Trafalgar Square, dedicated to St Martin of Tours, it is first mentioned in 1222 and was rebuilt by Henry VIII in 1542, then standing alone between the cities of Westminster and London. The present building is by James Gibbs. It flies the White Ensign of the Royal Navy and hosts concerts.
summaries.Q1481002: Opened on 24 May 1906 by César Ritz, creator of the Hotel Ritz in Paris, this luxury establishment of 133 rooms stands in Piccadilly and looks onto Green Park. Its exterior, of classical French inspiration, is by Charles Mewès and Davis, its interior decorated in the Louis XVI style. Margaret Thatcher died there on 8 April 2013.
summaries.Q1868965: In St Martin's Lane, in the City of Westminster, this theatre opened in 1904 is one of the largest in London; it was designed by the architect Frank Matcham for the impresario Oswald Stoll. The Sadler's Wells Opera Company moved in there in 1968, became the English National Opera in 1974 and bought the building for 12.8 million pounds.
summaries.Q38778: A Soho shopping street, near Oxford Street and Regent Street, it was laid out in the 1680s and takes its name from a house, Karnaby House. John Stephen opened his first shop there, His Clothes, in 1958; in the 1960s it became an emblem of Swinging London. It has been pedestrian since 1973.
summaries.Q1069141: Linking the two banks of the Thames between Grosvenor Bridge and Albert Bridge, it replaces an earlier suspension bridge designed by Thomas Page. It is the first self anchored suspension bridge built in the United Kingdom: its holding cables are not anchored in the ground. It was opened on 6 May 1937 by the Prime Minister of Canada, Mackenzie King.
summaries.Q2319878: This residential estate of the City of London is a concrete maze typical of the 1970s, with its pedestrian deck, its pools and towers of several dozen floors. The name comes from the French barbacane, rampart: a remnant of the Roman wall can be seen there and the remains of a medieval tower, as well as the rebuilt church of St Giles.
summaries.Q2896743: This Whitehall memorial was at first a temporary structure of wood and plaster, designed by Edwin Lutyens for the victory parade of 19 July 1919. Public pressure led to its replacement by a replica in Portland stone, which King George V unveiled on 11 November 1920. A commemoration is held there each Remembrance Sunday.
summaries.Q207385: This royal residence in the district of Kensington and Chelsea was built at the start of the 17th century as Nottingham House. William III bought it in 1689, wanting to live away from the bad air of the capital, and Christopher Wren enlarged it. Victoria was born there and lived there until July 1837, just after her accession. Part can be visited.
summaries.Q12110695: A museum housed in Somerset House, on the Strand, the gallery shows the collection of the Courtauld Institute, an institution of the University of London devoted to art history. Formed largely of gifts and bequests, it runs from the Middle Ages to the modern era and is valued for its French Impressionist and post-Impressionist paintings.
summaries.Q1137916: This neo-Georgian mansion in Regent's Park has been the official residence of the United States ambassador to the United Kingdom since 1955. The American heiress Barbara Hutton bought and then demolished the burnt out villa on the site, and had the present house built, which she sold after the war to the American government for a symbolic dollar.
summaries.Q1130266: This official London residence of the Archbishop of Canterbury stands on the south bank of the Thames, a little upstream from the Palace of Westminster, which occupies the other bank. The archbishopric acquired it around 1200. The oldest part is the Gothic chapel; Cardinal John Morton built the Tudor style brick gatehouse in 1495.
summaries.Q746639: This five star Strand hotel opened in 1889, built by Richard D'Oyly Carte, owner of the Savoy Theatre next door. It was the world's first public building lit by electricity. César Ritz first ran it and Auguste Escoffier created peach Melba there. Savoy Court, leading to it, is the only street in the United Kingdom where you drive on the right.
summaries.Q1169370: This non profit theatre in Chelsea opened in 1870; the present building was finished in 1888. It housed the new drama revolution at the beginning of the 20th century, then that of the 1950s. In 1956 it was bought by the English Stage Company, which is mainly interested in contemporary theatre.
summaries.Q1631609: Parallel to Regent Street, this Mayfair street was laid out from 1732 on land of Richard Boyle, 3rd Earl of Burlington. It is known for its made to measure, or bespoke, tailors: about 7,000 suits are made there each year. At no 3, the Beatles set up the offices of Apple Corps and gave their rooftop concert.
summaries.Q1241240: The first commercial exchange of the City of London, founded in 1565 by Thomas Gresham, who took up the idea of his father Richard and gave it a trapezoidal form inspired by the Antwerp exchange. Destroyed by the great fire of 1666, then burnt in 1838, it was each time rebuilt. It has housed luxury shops since 2001.
summaries.Q125555724: Raised in 1878 in Fleet Street, this monument by Charles Bell Birch carries the effigies of Queen Victoria and of her son the future Edward VII, under a bronze dragon wrongly called the Griffin. It stands on the site of a Christopher Wren gate demolished the same year and marks symbolically the boundary with the City of Westminster.
summaries.Q674773: Founded in 1857 from the collection of the Royal Society of Arts and the surplus of the Great Exhibition, this Kensington museum only became independent in 1909. It keeps more than 300,000 objects, among them Stephenson's Rocket, the command module of Apollo 10 and working steam engines. Entry has been free since 2001.
summaries.Q1628509: A home for veterans founded by a decree of Charles II in 1681, it was designed by Christopher Wren on the model of the Hôtel des Invalides and finished in 1692, when the first patients were admitted. Open to women since 2009, it has hosted the Chelsea Flower Show since 1913. The central building and the chapel can be visited.
summaries.Q123738: It is the largest park in central London and one of its royal parks. Its 140 hectares are separated from Kensington Gardens by the Serpentine. Henry VIII took the land back from the abbots of Westminster Abbey in 1536, and Decimus Burton designed a large part of it in the 1820s. Speakers' Corner occupies the north east part.
summaries.Q922967: The fourth church on the site, it is the oldest Gothic building in London: the previous building having burnt in 1212, construction ran from 1220 to 1420. Reduced to the rank of parish church after the dissolution of the monasteries in 1539, it was only raised to cathedral in 1905. Fellow players of Shakespeare rest there.
summaries.Q961148: An informal poultry market was held from 1321 near the Leadenhall manor, which the Lord Mayor Simon Eyre turned into a market in 1445. It was roofed after the great fire of 1666. Horace Jones gave it its wrought iron and glazed structure in 1881. It served as Diagon Alley in Harry Potter and the Philosopher's Stone.
summaries.Q2165797: A West End theatre in The Strand, it opened on 10 October 1881, built by Richard D'Oyly Carte on the site of the old Savoy Palace. It is the first theatre in the world to have adopted electric lighting. D'Oyly Carte had the Savoy Hotel built next door in 1889.
summaries.Q1996213: A crossing of Regent Street and Oxford Street, the place designed by John Nash bore at its opening the name Regent Circus North. In 1969 Elizabeth II took the controls of a train from Green Park to open the Victoria line, which makes her the only British monarch to have travelled publicly on the city's underground.
summaries.Q894072: A wholesale and retail food market in Southwark, in south east London, it is one of the largest and oldest food markets in the world. Wholesale trading is held every weekday morning between 2 am and 8 am, retail on Thursdays, Fridays and Saturdays. On 3 June 2017 a terrorist attack struck the market.
summaries.Q547654: Raised in Park Lane, this memorial pays tribute to the animals that served and died under British command through history. Designed by the English sculptor David Backhouse, it was unveiled on 24 November 2004 by the Princess Royal, Anne. The inscription ends with these words: “They had no choice.”
summaries.Q238587: Opened in 1856 in central London, this art museum brings together portraits of British historical figures, chosen not for their maker but for the sitter's fame. The collections mix paintings, prints, photographs, caricatures, drawings and sculptures. Portraits of living people have been admitted since 1969.
summaries.Q2505545: This London mansion stands near St James's Palace, Buckingham Palace and the Palace of Westminster. The architect John Vardy, a former pupil of William Kent, built it in 1756 for the first Earl Spencer. It is today open to the public and can be hired for events, among them weddings.
summaries.Q270263: Opened on 27 April 1828 to the north of Regent's Park, in the City of Westminster, it is the oldest scientific zoo in the world. On 15 hectares it houses more than 20,000 animals belonging to 260 species, among them more than a hundred endangered species. It opened the first reptile house and the first public aquarium.
summaries.Q1429312: Built in the 12th century between Fleet Street and the Thames by and for the knights of the Order of the Temple, it is dedicated to St Mary. Its round nave draws on the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, and its effigies are famous. Since 1608 it has served as the chapel of two Inns of Court, the Inner Temple and the Middle Temple.
summaries.Q498563: A luxury goods department store in central London, it was set up in 1707 at 181 Piccadilly by William Fortnum and Hugh Mason. At first a grocery, it built its reputation on quality food and grew fast in the Victorian era. A clock of four tonnes, commissioned in 1964, stands above the main entrance.
summaries.Q4780361: Devoted above all to musicals, this theatre in Shaftesbury Avenue, in the City of Westminster, opened its doors in 1901 and is among the listed buildings. On 19 December 2013 part of the auditorium ceiling collapsed during a performance, injuring more than 75 people.
summaries.Q1194528: A long street in the district of Tower Hamlets, in east London, it is mentioned under this name from 1550, because it passed near a place where earth was dug for bricks and tiles. The area has taken in Flemish, French and Jewish communities; the street now forms the heart of London's Bangladeshi and Indian quarter.
summaries.Q212834: Nicknamed The Walkie-Talkie for its shape, this glass and steel skyscraper was built from 2009 to the end of 2014 by Rafael Viñoly, for more than 200 million pounds. It rises to 160 metres, against the 200 planned. Its concave windows concentrated the sun's rays in the neighbouring streets, which led to protective screens being fitted.
summaries.Q1439502: Antonio Canova sculpted between 1802 and 1806 this heroic nude in white marble, 3.45 m high, showing Mars with the features of Napoleon I. The emperor refused it in 1811, judging it too athletic. Bought in 1816 by the British government, it was offered the same year to the Duke of Wellington and stands at the foot of the staircase at Apsley House.
summaries.Q270920: Founded in 1768 by a personal act of King George III, this independent institution, funded privately, promotes the visual arts through exhibitions and teaching. It brings together elected artists and has sat at Burlington House, in Piccadilly, since its centenary in 1868. Its first president was the painter Joshua Reynolds.
summaries.Q2723633: Charles Dickens lived in this Georgian house at 48 Doughty Street, in Bloomsbury, between 1837 and 1839, as his literary career took off; there he wrote Oliver Twist and Nicholas Nickleby among others. Threatened with disappearance in 1923, the house was bought and restored by The Dickens Fellowship, which made it a museum in 1925.
summaries.Q216914: The oldest of London's royal parks covers 23 hectares between The Mall, the Horse Guards, Birdcage Walk and Buckingham Palace Road. Henry VIII bought this marshy area in 1532; James I had it drained and put exotic animals there, and Charles II opened it to the public. Its lake has two islands, one of them Duck Island.
summaries.Q1811339: Also called the Regent's Park Mosque, it occupies land given in 1944 by the British government to the Muslim community. Designed by Frederick Gibberd, it was finished in July 1977, for 6 million pounds partly raised by gifts from King Faisal. Topped by a golden dome, it has been Grade II* listed since 2018.
summaries.Q2749941: This luxury hotel at no 53 Park Lane, in Mayfair, opened in 1931 on the site of Dorchester House, a palace demolished in 1929. General Eisenhower stayed there during the Second World War. The establishment belongs to the Dorchester group, owned by the Sultan of Brunei, and was the target of boycott campaigns in 2013 and then in 2019.
summaries.Q540426: This West End theatre, built in 1720, is the third oldest in London still in use. Samuel Foote took over the lease in 1747, then a royal patent allowed him in 1766 to play drama during the summer. The original building stood further north; redesigned by John Nash, the theatre has been on its present site since 1821.
summaries.Q169430: A shopping street in the St James's area, between Haymarket and St James's Street, it is known for its English shirtmakers and its menswear shops. It owes its name to Henry Jermyn, 1st Earl of St Albans, closely involved in the development of the area. Isaac Newton lived there, at no 88 and then 87.
summaries.Q1613853: At 110 Bishopsgate, this City skyscraper belongs to Heron International and was designed by the architects of Kohn Pedersen Fox. Work began in April 2008; a ceremony marked the completion of the structure on 12 April 2010, and the mast added on 22 July brought the height to 230 metres.
summaries.Q6906912: Raised in Whitehall, near the Cenotaph, this monument pays tribute to the women who took part in the war effort during the Second World War by taking over the work of men. Designed by John W. Mills, it was unveiled in the presence of Elizabeth II in July 2005 and is made up of different workers' uniforms.
summaries.Q749808: Created in 1917, this national body of British military museums has five sites, three of them in London. The main and most visited one occupies the central part of the former Bethlem Royal Hospital: it deals with the First and the Second World War, as well as with Nazism.
summaries.Q2339207: A group of concert halls created after the Second World War, it lies along the Thames, between County Hall and Waterloo Bridge, and brings together three main buildings: the Royal Festival Hall, the Queen Elizabeth Hall and the Hayward Gallery. It runs an area including the Purcell Room, the Jubilee Gardens and The Queen's Walk.
summaries.Q739341: One of London's royal parks, it is shared between the City of Westminster and the borough of Camden. Its name refers to George, Prince Regent, who asked the architect John Nash to draw up a plan for the former Marylebone Park when the lease ran out in 1811. Its 166 hectares hold London Zoo and a lake.
summaries.Q1938714: The parish church of the Tower of London, it was built from 1519 by Sir Richard Cholmondeley for Henry VIII, on the site of a chapel earlier than the Norman conquest. Its fame rests on the burials of prisoners executed at the Tower, among them three queens: Anne Boleyn, Catherine Howard and Lady Jane Grey.
summaries.Q3237793: Arthur Lasenby Liberty opened in Regent Street in 1875 a fabric shop, at first called Emporium because it offered goods imported from the British Empire. In 1884 came the Liberty brand, a fine cotton with floral patterns. The department store occupies numbers 214-220 and keeps its Tudor front of 1924 on Great Marlborough Street.
summaries.Q129143: A Westminster square whose name, taken in 1830, commemorates the battle of Trafalgar of 1805. Its layout, designed by John Nash, began in the 1820s on the site of the old royal stables and was finished in the 1840s. Nelson's Column, raised in 1842, reaches 44 m and four bronze lions have surrounded it since 1867.
summaries.Q1631720: Created at the end of the 19th century to improve traffic in the area, this thoroughfare links Piccadilly Circus to New Oxford Street and crosses Charing Cross Road at Cambridge Circus. It belongs to the West End theatre district: the Lyric, Apollo, Gielgud and Queens theatres follow one another on its north side.
summaries.Q922589: At 201 Bishopsgate, in the City, this skyscraper designed by the architects Skidmore, Owings & Merrill was built by British Land between 2005 and 2009. Its 165 metres and its 35 floors make it the fifth tallest skyscraper of the City of London.
summaries.Q2919484: On the Victoria Embankment, by the Thames, this sculpture pays tribute to those who took part in the Battle of Britain. More than 24 metres long, the monument designed by Bill Bond carries the names of all the participants; the bronze reliefs are by the sculptor Paul Day.
summaries.Q195436: Set in the Millbank area, on the site of a former prison, the museum opened on 21 July 1897 under the name National Gallery of British Art. It bears the name of its patron, the industrialist Henry Tate, officially took that of Tate Gallery in 1932, then that of Tate Britain in March 2000.
summaries.Q119892: This central London park, one of the royal parks, lies between Hyde Park and St James's Park. Marshy ground where the lepers of St James's hospital were buried, it was enclosed in the 16th century by Henry VIII, then Charles II made it a royal park in 1668. Triangular in shape, it is made up entirely of woodland.
summaries.Q2301992: This church of the City of London, in Cheapside, is known for its bells, the Bow bells: a cockney is a person born where they can be heard ringing. Destroyed by the great fire of 1666, it was rebuilt by Christopher Wren. Wrecked by the Blitz in 1941, it was restored from 1956 and reconsecrated in 1964.
summaries.Q768935: In Langham Place, in St Marylebone, this grand hotel faces All Souls church. Designed by John Giles, it was opened on 10 June 1865 by the Prince of Wales, the future Edward VII, and was then the largest hotel in the capital. Bombed during the Second World War, it was turned into offices before reopening in 1991.
summaries.Q215255: This Westminster junction, created in 1819 as a continuation of Regent Street, brings together five major West End thoroughfares. It is known for its illuminated signs and for the Shaftesbury Memorial fountain, put up in 1893 in honour of the philanthropist Lord Shaftesbury and topped by the Angel of Christian Charity, known as Eros.
summaries.Q773458: North of Oxford Street, in the City of Westminster, the street links Marylebone Road to Wigmore Street and bears the name of Edward Harley, 2nd Earl of Oxford, who developed these lands. Doctors settled there in the 1860s: more than 3,000 people now work there in practices, clinics and hospitals.
summaries.Q2389056: This skyscraper in the Camden area rises at 286 Euston Road, at the junction of Tottenham Court Road and Euston Road. 124 m high, it has 36 floors. Sydney Kaye designed it in 1970.
summaries.Q3497572: It shows Oliver Cromwell, Lord Protector of the Commonwealth of England, Scotland and Ireland, and stands outside the House of Commons, at Westminster. Put up in 1899, it is the work of the sculptor Hamo Thornycroft.
summaries.Q653858: A cultural centre in the north of the City of London, at the heart of the Barbican Estate, it is the largest performing arts centre in Europe: concerts, theatre, cinema, exhibitions and library. The London Symphony Orchestra and the BBC Symphony Orchestra are based there. Designed in the 1960s, built in the 1970s, it opened in 1982.
summaries.Q62408: Seat of the Parliament of the United Kingdom, it lines the north bank of the Thames, in the City of Westminster. A fire destroyed it almost entirely on 16 October 1834, sparing Westminster Hall. Charles Barry rebuilt it in neo-Gothic style from 1840. Its Clock Tower, called the Elizabeth Tower since 2012, holds the bell Big Ben.
summaries.Q822607: The former private gardens of Kensington Palace, they form one of London's royal parks, immediately west of Hyde Park, over 1.1 km2. Enclosed, they have kept the Round Pond and hold the Albert Memorial, the statue of Peter Pan and the Serpentine Gallery. J. M. Barrie set Peter Pan in Kensington Gardens there.
summaries.Q2038269: The official church of the Royal Air Force, at the east end of the Strand, it was rebuilt by Christopher Wren from 1680 to 1682, its steeple added by James Gibbs from 1719 to 1720. Bombed on 10 May 1941, it kept its outer walls and its tower; a fire gutted the interior. Its Welsh slate floor carries RAF badges.
summaries.Q608175: This skyscraper of 101 metres, built in 1963, houses a hotel of 512 rooms of the Hilton chain. It was then one of the tallest buildings in the United Kingdom. Its architects are the William Tabler practice and the practice of Lewis Solomon, Kaye & Partners.
summaries.Q192687: For more than two hundred years this Westminster street has held the residences of the British Prime Minister, at number 10, and of the Chancellor of the Exchequer, at 11; number 12, the former residence of the chief whip, now serves as the Prime Minister's press office. Public access has been barred since 1982.
summaries.Q893034: This street of the St James's area, in the City of Westminster, runs from Coventry Street to Pall Mall. Its name comes from the hay market. It is part of the theatre district, the West End, and has hosted theatres since the 17th century, among them the Theatre Royal, built by John Nash in 1820, and Her Majesty's Theatre.
summaries.Q852282: Grade II listed, the building occupies the south end of Kingsway, between Aldwych and the Strand. It housed the headquarters of the BBC World Service until its departure for Broadcasting House in 2012, and since 2015 belongs, for the most part, to the Strand campus of King's College London.
summaries.Q7373706: At Hyde Park Corner, this monument unveiled in 1925 pays tribute to the 49,076 soldiers of the Royal Artillery killed during the First World War. Created in 1918, the regiment's memorial fund called for a visual representation of artillery that no architect approached was able to supply; Charles Sargeant Jagger's design was accepted in 1922.
summaries.Q757178: A Town class light cruiser of the Royal Navy, launched in 1938, it opened fire on a German battery at Ver-sur-Mer on 6 June 1944, then served during the Korean War. It is one of the only British ships of the Second World War preserved; it is moored on the Thames, near London Bridge station.
summaries.Q169101: Official residence and workplace of the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, in the City of Westminster. The address is officially that of the First Lord of the Treasury, a post held jointly with that of Prime Minister since 1905. George II gave it in 1732 to Robert Walpole, who insisted the gift go to the office and not to him.
summaries.Q1069148: Created in 1673 by the Worshipful Society of Apothecaries under the name Apothecaries' Garden, it is the second oldest botanic garden in Great Britain, after the one in Oxford. Its high brick walls shelter the largest fruiting olive tree in the country. Long kept by the Society, it only opened to the general public in 1983.
summaries.Q851924: Built in 1701 by the Sephardic community of London, Jews originally from Spain and Portugal, it is the oldest synagogue in the United Kingdom still in use, Grade I listed. The interior decoration reflects the influence of the Portuguese synagogue in Amsterdam. The roof, destroyed by a fire in 1738, was rebuilt in 1749.
summaries.Q4975949: This Mayfair hotel, at no 33 Albemarle Street, occupies a run of Georgian houses in white stucco. Passed to the Rocco Forte Hotels group in 2003, it reopened on 9 April 2018 after refurbishment. Rudyard Kipling wrote The Jungle Book there and Alexander Graham Bell made the first telephone call in Europe there.
summaries.Q214820: This City of Westminster thoroughfare runs from Parliament Square to Charing Cross and gathers so many ministries that its name stands, by metonymy, for the British government. The name comes from Whitehall Palace, destroyed almost entirely by a fire in 1698; the Banqueting House is its only remnant.
summaries.Q2716065: This street of the City of London, next to Eastcheap, held the bakery of Thomas Farriner, where the Great Fire of London began in September 1666; a plaque marks the spot. According to the chronicler John Stow, its name would come from puddings, a term then meaning the entrails discarded by the butchers of Eastcheap.
summaries.Q2339039: An office skyscraper at 101-103 New Oxford Street, next to St Giles' Circus, in the Camden area. Designed by George Marsh, of the firm Richard Seifert and Partners, it was built from 1963 to 1966 by Wimpey Construction. 117 m high with 32 floors, it is among the first skyscrapers raised in London.
summaries.Q2911131: A monument to Prince Frederick, Duke of York and Albany, second son of George III, commander in chief of the British army. On his death in 1827 the whole army gave a day's pay to raise this column for him; Benjamin Dean Wyatt's plan was chosen in December 1830. Hollow, it holds a stair of 168 steps.
summaries.Q642039: A former part of Whitehall Palace, designed by Inigo Jones in 1619 and finished in 1622 with the help of John Webb. It has a single room on two levels, whose coffered ceiling received paintings by Rubens commissioned by Charles I in 1635. The king was beheaded in front of the building on 30 January 1649.
summaries.Q272162: Built between 1531 and 1536 for Henry VIII on the site of a former leper hospital dedicated to St James, this red brick Tudor palace is arranged around four courts. The sovereigns have not lived there since 1837, the year of Victoria's accession, but it remains the administrative heart of the Crown.
summaries.Q1471930: An artificial lake of eleven hectares laid out in Hyde Park: in 1730 Queen Caroline, wife of George II, ordered a dam on the river Westbourne, today underground. Strictly speaking, the name covers only the part east of the bridge, the western half being called the Long Water. The greatest depth is 12 metres.
summaries.Q81473: A multi purpose Methodist building put up from 1905 to 1911 facing Westminster Abbey, on the site of the old Royal Aquarium, for the centenary of the death of John Wesley. Designed by Edwin Alfred Rickards, it makes early use of reinforced concrete in Great Britain. It housed the first part of the first United Nations General Assembly.
summaries.Q5911940: Opened in 1900 under the name Hotel Russell, this five star hotel in Russell Square is the work of Charles Fitzroy Doll, an architect who also designed the dining room of the Titanic: the hotel restaurant is held to be almost identical to it. Four statues of British queens, by Henry Charles Fehr, stand above the main entrance.
summaries.Q848912: Laid out in the 1670s, this pedestrian West End square was at first a garden facing Leicester House, the town palace of the Sydneys, earls of Leicester, the title from which it takes its name. A famous lawsuit, Tulk v Moxhay, in 1848, largely explains its preservation. It is today lined with large cinemas.
summaries.Q1432321: A City thoroughfare that runs from the Bank of England to Gracechurch Street. It owes its name to the goldsmiths and pawnbrokers who came from Lombardy, to whom Edward I granted the land in the 13th century. Lloyd's Coffee House, ancestor of Lloyd's of London, stood there from 1691 to 1785; a plaque marks the site.
